query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At operating temperatures between 400°C and 600°C, the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by the in situ formation of a stable, self-healing, high-hardness oxide layer that protects the coating from rapid wear and delamination.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings deposited on conventional metal substrates with nanocrystalline or partially amorphous microstructure typical of sputter- or vapor-deposited films.
generation.intervention: A mild pre-oxidation treatment (controlled annealing in a low-oxygen atmosphere) applied prior to wear testing to promote the formation of a uniform and adherent oxide layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear conditions with testing temperatures in the range of 400°C–600°C under fixed loading regimes that simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: An adherent, self-healing oxide layer that forms on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: The pre-oxidation treatment accelerates the oxidation kinetics, leading to the formation of a high-hardness oxide phase that fills microcracks and mitigates further wear; during high-temperature wear, this oxide acts as a barrier, reducing friction and preventing coating delamination.
generation.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized coating will exhibit a significantly lower wear rate, reduced friction coefficient, and enhanced resistance to delamination compared to the baseline untreated coating due to the protective oxide layer.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings without pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: Results are expected to hold under high-temperature (400°C–600°C) wear conditions and controlled mechanical loading, and may not extend to significantly lower or higher temperatures or vastly different loading environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise nature of the oxide composition, its long-term stability, and the kinetics of its self-healing behavior remain uncertain and may be sensitive to subtle changes in processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical conventional metal substrates, one with a mild pre-oxidation treatment and one without. Subject both sets to identical wear testing under high-temperature conditions (400°C–600°C) at fixed loads. Use microscopy and surface analysis (e.g., SEM, XPS) to evaluate oxide layer formation and adherence, and measure wear rates and friction coefficients.
measurements: Wear rate (mass or volume loss per unit distance/time)
Coefficient of friction during wear testing
Oxide layer thickness and continuity (via SEM/XPS)
Degree of coating delamination or crack propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit a detectable, uniform, adherent oxide layer or if their measured wear rates and friction coefficients are statistically indistinguishable from (or worse than) those of the untreated coatings, then the hypothesis that the oxide layer governs the improved wear resistance would be falsified.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

frame.system: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings deposited on conventional metal substrates, with the microstructure (e.g., nanocrystalline or partially amorphous) typical of sputter‐ or vapor‐deposited films.
frame.goal: To understand the mechanistic basis for the overall high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
frame.limitation: Prior studies mainly focused on room-temperature wear and isolated alloy characteristics (composition, grain size) rather than the integrated, temperature‐dependent wear response of a thin-film coating on a substrate.
constraints: FeNiCrCoCu must remain as a thin protective coating (not bulk)
Application is for high-temperature wear conditions
Economic considerations restrict it to use as a coating on conventional metals
frame.regime: Elevated temperatures (e.g., 400°C to 600°C) under controlled wear loading that simulates high-temperature service conditions.
prior_attempts: Investigations primarily examined static properties such as composition and grain size or limited room-temperature wear tests, which did not adequately address the dynamic interaction and performance of the coating across an extended high-temperature range.
frame.understanding: Hypothesis: At high temperatures, the overall wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu coating is governed by its ability to form a stable, high-hardness oxide layer (or modified nanostructure) that acts as a self-healing barrier during wear processes. Intervention: Introduce a mild pre-oxidation or surface treatment step to promote the selective formation and adhesion of a protective oxide phase relative to a baseline untreated coating. Expected Observations: Under high-temperature wear testing (400°C–600°C) and fixed loading conditions, the treated coating should exhibit a significantly lower wear rate and enhanced resistance against coating delamination compared to the baseline. The protective oxide layer should remain adherent and contribute to a lower friction coefficient. Connection to Prior Evidence: Room-temperature studies imply that microstructural factors (e.g., grain size and composition) influence wear, and this hypothesis extends that reasoning by positing that high-temperature oxidation behavior is the key mechanism, building on observed oxide formation in similar systems. Falsification Criterion: If high-temperature wear testing fails to reveal the formation of the expected stable oxide layer or if the treated coating does not show any reduction in wear rate (or even degrades further compared to the baseline), then the hypothesis would be falsified.
